title: Post-Scarcity Leads to Technological Stagnation
gist: Rosenbauer argues Moore's Law was always an economic phenomenon rather than a physical one, and that the binding constraint on semiconductors is now demand-side imagination, not fabrication physics. With mask costs running $1M at 28nm to $40M at 3nm, leading-edge fabs consolidated to TSMC and Samsung, and LLMs the only application with an uncapped hardware appetite, he warns the AI buildout is a wager that could leave trillion-dollar fabs as textbook overproduction and stall Moore's Law outright.

insights.claim: Wirth's law — software getting less efficient faster than hardware gets more efficient — means most consumer compute gains are absorbed by bloat rather than converted into new capability.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Hardware upgrade cycles driven by software bloat are demand of low quality — it does not create new application categories, so it cannot sustain leading-edge fab economics.

insights.claim: For the average person, compute is available in such abundance that it exceeds our knowledge of how to put it to productive use, with modern text editing doing little that a thirty-year-old machine with a million times less computing power could not.

insights.claim: Gordon Moore's central warning was that his law was a result of economics, not physics, so the future of computing will be determined by our ability to conceptualize uses for compute rather than by our ability to innovate technologically.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Reframes semiconductor forecasting as a demand-modeling problem — track application creation, not transistor roadmaps, to time the cycle.
insights.quote: the future of computing will be determined not by our ability to innovate technologically, but by our ability to conceptualize what this compute would be used for.

insights.claim: Early computing's core workload, bureaucracy, is overwhelmingly linear and was rapidly overwhelmed by exponential compute growth — a modern laptop can process facts about the entire world's population in under an hour — yet pen-and-paper artifacts like signatures persist, with DocuSign employing 7,000 people despite public-key cryptography solving the problem decades ago.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Institutional inertia, not technical capability, defines enterprise software TAM — incumbents can persist long after their problem is technically solved, and their moats are procedural rather than computational.
insights.quote: Public-key cryptography solved this problem properly decades ago; DocuSign still has 7,000 employees today.

themes.theme: LLMs as the Only Uncapped Compute Sink

insights.claim: The large language model is the first consumer application in decades whose appetite for hardware has no visible ceiling, with hundreds of millions of people routing questions, drafts and small work tasks through chatbots that are absorbing search, customer service and a growing share of clerical labor.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: LLM demand is the load-bearing assumption for the entire compute buildout — if it caps out, there is no successor application queued behind it.
insights.quote: The large language model is the first consumer application in decades whose appetite for hardware has no visible ceiling

insights.claim: Current AI usage — customer-service agents, automated Excel spreadsheets, low-level software engineering — sits uneasily with the claim that every firm will run autonomous agents consuming tokens by the billions.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: The gap between demonstrated enterprise usage and the token-consumption forecasts underwriting capex is the key thing to monitor for a demand air-pocket.
insights.quote: the claim that every firm will see autonomous agents that consume tokens by the billions sits uneasily with these prevailing uses.

insights.claim: For LLMs, inference has now overtaken training in total compute cost, an instance of arbitrary scaling where more resources solve bigger problems of the same kind rather than opening new problem classes.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: The compute mix shifting to inference changes hardware requirements and margin structure — it favors inference-optimized silicon and makes demand track usage volumes rather than model release cycles.

themes.theme: Gaming's Exhausted Demand Curve as Precedent

insights.claim: The GPU lineage ran from 1970s-80s blitters offloading repetitive graphics work, to 1990s dedicated polygon hardware, to early-2000s shaders justifying processors for bulk processing of simple arbitrary functions, culminating in NVIDIA's 1999 GeForce 256 marketed as the world's first GPU.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: General-purpose accelerators historically emerge from a consumer workload with insatiable demand, then get repurposed — a template for spotting where the next compute sink originates.
insights.quote: In 1999, NVIDIA released the GeForce 256, marketing it as the world’s first GPU and a revolution in video game graphics.
insights.locator: In 1999, NVIDIA released the GeForce 256

insights.claim: Gaming accelerators spread into science and engineering within a few years of the GPU's debut, making protein-folding simulations at least twenty times faster on general-purpose gaming technology.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Cross-domain spillover from a consumer-scale hardware market is what makes advanced silicon economically viable — losing the consumer volume base removes the subsidy for scientific compute.
insights.quote: Protein-folding simulations became at least twenty times faster thanks to general-purpose gaming technology.
insights.locator: Within a few years, these gaming accelerators

insights.claim: Video games no longer offer an obvious opportunity to push computing demand: ray tracing is achievable on consumer hardware, photorealism is now bottlenecked by prohibitively expensive artist labor for no obviously greater spectacle, and the indie industry has grown on stylized art that is cheap to produce and cheap to render.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Gaming is a worked example of a compute-demand engine exhausting itself for economic rather than technical reasons — the same failure mode threatens AI demand.
insights.quote: Because of this, there is no obvious remaining opportunity for video games to push computing demand.

themes.theme: Fab Economics: Exponential Costs, Collapsing Competition

insights.claim: Fab construction has escalated from a few billion dollars a decade ago to modern campuses pushing into the hundreds of billions, while in the 1970s and 1980s it was common for small chip startups to own their own fabs and TSMC's pure-play foundry model did not appear until 1987, nineteen years after Intel's founding.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Quantifies the capital-intensity trend that determines how many players can stay at the node frontier — and how quickly the count goes to near zero.
insights.quote: Ten years ago, a fabrication plant for microchips may have cost a few billion dollars to build. Today, modern fab campuses are getting pushed into the hundreds of billions.
insights.locator: It is not just the history of gaming

insights.claim: Photolithography mask costs have risen from $1 million for 28-nanometer chips to $10 million at 7 nm and $40 million at 3 nm, pricing startups out of tapeouts and threatening to push foundry prices beyond what fabless customers can afford.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Hard numbers on the fixed-cost barrier: leading-edge design is consolidating into a handful of buyers, which concentrates foundry customer risk and shrinks silicon startup formation.
insights.quote: from $1 million for 28-nanometer chips, to $10 million for 7 nm, to $40 million for 3 nm.
insights.locator: The masks used in the photolithography processes

insights.claim: Leading-edge fabrication has consolidated to TSMC and Samsung after Intel fell behind and required heavy U.S. government subsidies, while AMD's spun-off GlobalFoundries formally exited competition on the most advanced manufacturing processes.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: A two-player leading edge with a state-subsidized third is a structurally fragile supply chain and a geopolitical concentration risk for every AI compute forecast.
insights.quote: While there used to be dozens of companies at the bleeding edge, today, the leading chip fabs include only TSMC and Samsung
insights.locator: While there used to be dozens of companies

insights.claim: Semiconductor survivorship is largely a matter of surviving rounds of industrial Russian roulette across process transitions, since companies that bet wrong on a manufacturing process are commonly removed from the cutting edge permanently.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Node transitions are the discrete events where competitive position is won or lost forever — the correct moments to reprice foundry and IDM equity.
insights.quote: real men own fabs

insights.claim: It is a serious possibility that pushing semiconductor technology further will exceed what even the most deep-pocketed nation-states can pay, with a decade's extrapolation implying fab costs in the trillions and approximately zero companies able to keep up.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: If true, the terminal state of Moore's Law is a fiscal ceiling rather than a physics ceiling — and compute-cost curves underpinning AI models would flatten a decade earlier than assumed.
insights.quote: Extrapolating these trends another decade suggests fab costs in the trillions of dollars and approximately zero companies that can keep up.

insights.claim: AI companies raise large sums on hype while their actual profitability is questionable and some industry leaders have accused them of overcharging, making it unclear that LLMs alone can justify building a trillion-dollar superfab.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Directly links AI monetization to the viability of the next node — weak LLM economics propagate backward into foundry capex decisions.
insights.quote: it’s not clear that LLMs alone will be nearly sufficient to justify building a trillion-dollar superfab.

insights.claim: AI scaling laws provide a roadmap for justifying a superfab, but their exponential nature may outrun fab technology so that compute requirements and costs grow faster than revenue.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: The scaling-law bull case contains its own limiter: if cost curves outpace revenue curves, the roadmap terminates on unit economics rather than capability.
insights.quote: The compute requirements, and by extension the costs, may grow faster than revenue.

insights.so_what: A usable model for judging whether an AI capability is a durable compute sink or a vein about to run out — test whether bigger instances of the same problem are worth more.

themes.theme: Overproduction, Ohno, and the Adoption Test

insights.claim: Rephrasing 'post-scarcity' as 'overproduction' places it in an old economic tradition running from John Stuart Mill to Toyota's Taiichi Ohno, who treated overproduction as a greater problem than underproduction because it reflects demand-pipeline inefficiency that compounds waste through overprocessing, transport, waiting and defects.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Applies lean-manufacturing waste categories to AI infrastructure — idle or misallocated compute is not neutral, it compounds cost through the stack.
insights.quote: The latter recognized overproduction as a greater problem than underproduction, because it reflects inefficiencies in the demand-production pipeline that lead to compounding waste through overprocessing, transport, waiting, and defects.
insights.locator: If we simply rephrase “post-scarcity” as “overproduction,”

insights.claim: Ohno's model let demand pull production, mirroring the American supermarket shelf restocked only as customers empty it, whereas AI scaling laws invite the opposite: compute yields capability with no guarantee the capability finds a buyer, making the trillion-dollar fab production running far ahead of any order.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: The sharpest framing of AI capex risk: supply-push manufacturing at unprecedented scale with no order book behind it.
insights.quote: The trillion-dollar fab is production running far ahead of any order.
insights.locator: Ohno’s preference was to let demand pull production

insights.claim: Genuinely useful technology sees widespread adoption even while primitive, so the argument that a technology needs to become much more convenient before adoption can occur is itself evidence of a lack of underlying value — as demonstrated by VR's failure to take hold during the metaverse boom.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: A fast diagnostic for hyped technologies: if adoption requires the product to first get much better, the value proposition is probably absent.
insights.quote: What separates useful from overbuilt technology is that the former sees widespread adoption even while primitive.
insights.locator: What separates useful from overbuilt technology

insights.claim: Moore's Law can and will grind to a halt if human innovation cannot find applications for the compute already produced, because advances in semiconductors slow in response to a lack of profitable scalability downstream of industrial society's aggregate demand.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Positions demand imagination as the leading indicator for the entire semiconductor complex — a stagnation scenario that no process roadmap would signal in advance.
insights.quote: Moore’s Law can and will grind to a halt if human innovation cannot find applications for the vast amount of compute we have produced.
insights.locator: Moore’s Law can and will grind to a halt

insights.claim: The main fallacy of the post-scarcity thesis is that human needs could equally have been declared satisfied after the twentieth-century agricultural revolutions or the spread of cars and air-conditioning; past a certain point technology develops only to serve desires beyond needs, so the future depends on people with a concrete desire to outstrip them.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: The bear case for a compute-abundant future is cultural, not technical — ambition is the scarce input, and its absence shows up as flat semiconductor demand.
insights.quote: After a certain point, technology develops only to account for desires beyond human needs.
insights.locator: The main fallacy of the post-scarcity thesis
